newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FOCUS - Israel markets shrug off interest rate blow.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Israel markets shrug off interest rate blow.

text.p: Israel's financial markets are girding themselves for new gains despite earlier disappointment at the lack of an interest rate cut in December, traders said on Tuesday.
"The reaction to the rate announcement was very moderate and investors are very optimistic now," said Izik Winish of Capital Securities about the stock market.
"After two days of profit-taking the market is ready for another rise. Most investors believe that in the short run the positive trend will continue."

The Bank of Israel announced on Monday, after the stock and bond markets closed, that its key lending rate would stay at an annualised 15.2 percent in December. The markets had been hoping for a cut of as much as 0.5 percentage point.

On the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, the benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares fell by 1.04 percent in early trading. But the index subsequently recovered slightly, ending down just 0.49 percent at 195.82 points.
Bond prices fell across the board but losses were less than expected, analysts said.
The shekel strengthened against the dollar in the local foreign currency market. The representative rate for the currency was fixed at 3.2420 shekels, compared with 3.2470 on Monday.

"The shekel started rising (on Monday) against the dollar immediately after the rate announcement, despite the dollar's rise against the mark," said a dealer at Israel Discount Bank. "On Tuesday, this trend continued but the rise was very moderate."

In spite of the markets' muted reaction, Israeli exporters say the central bank's firm monetary policy artificially boosts the shekel and is hurting competitiveness. "Companies are suffering from the low exchange rate," said Danny Alt, head of portfolios at Nesuah Trading and Investment.
One trader said the news that Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel was standing firm was not at all bad for foreign investors, who hold about 10 percent of the shares on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.

"All in all I would say for foreign investors such an announcement should be viewed as a positive one because it looks as if there is somebody standing alone and fighting inflation," said Eli Nahum, head of trading at Zannex Securities.
The central bank, concerned with inflation expected to reach 11 percent this year, says it cannot ease up on monetary policy until the government slashes spending.
Lawmakers are haggling over government proposals, due to be passed on December 31, to slash as much as seven billion shekels from the 1997 spending package.

"I would say that for the time being the reaction of the market seems to be much better than it could have been," Nahum said. "And I won't be surprised if the market will return to a positive trend within a few days."
